## Principal Components Analysis

- Let's build some intuition for PCA by starting with a picture:

.center[
  ![:scale 50%](./pca.png)
]

- On the left, we visualize the contents of a data frame with six rows (six data points) and two columns, $x_1$ and $x_2$

- What does the PCA algorithm do?  It uses linear algebra tools to move the coordinate system origin to the centroid of the point "cloud," then rotates the axes such that "PC 1" lies along the direction of greatest variation (i.e., along the points), and "PC 2" lies orthogonal to to "PC 1"

- In the end, **PCA is the linear transformation of a coordinate system**


---

## Principal Components Analysis

- But, there is actually more to PCA then just the transformation

.center[
  ![:scale 50%](./pca.png)
]

- On the right, we move into "PC space," where PC1 has become the $x$ axis, etc.

- Note how the data all lie along the PC1 axis

  + in PC space, we can see that the true space of the data is one-dimensional: including a (the) second dimension would add no statistical information at all
  
  + we *could* visualize and interpret the data using, e.g., a histogram of PC1 values, ignoring PC2 entirely

- So in the end, PCA is also a *dimensionality-reduction tool*


---

## Why Would We Use PCA?

- There are two primary reasons to use PCA:

  + it can assist data visualization: if the predictor data lie within a subspace of the native space of the data, we can just visualize the data in that subspace

  + it can assist statistical inference: PCA "decorrelates" the data $-$ there is no linear association between the data along PC1 and PC2, etc. $-$ so **multicollinearity is mitigated**!

- **NOTE: PCA is not appropriate for use with categorical data!**


---

## PCA: It's a Linear Algorithm

- The main limitation of PCA is that it is a *linear* algorithm: it projects data to hyperplanes

.center[
  ![:scale 25%](./swiss_roll.png)
]

- These data lie on a curving two-dimensional strip embedded in a three-dimensional space

  + projecting these data to any two-dimensional plane or one-dimensional line would effectively discard a large portion of the statistical information they contain

  + for visualization and/or learning, we could explore the use of *nonlinear* techniques like diffusion maps, local linear embedding, self-organizing maps, $t$-SNE, etc.


---

## PCA: It's Not Factor Analysis

- PCA is a closely related to a family of algorithms commonly dubbed *factor analyses*, and, for instance, some works will use the phrases "PCA" and "factor analysis" interchangeably

- The PCA algorithm, *as described here*, is a **deterministic algorithm** $-$ it just ingests the data values as they are and produces a result, full stop

- *Exploratory factor analysis* (EFA) is a variant of PCA which *does* attempt to take the random variability of the data into account

  + it maps the $p$ observed variables to $k < p$ *factors*; "exploratory" means we do not know *a priori* how that mapping may occur

- *Confirmatory factor analysis* basically adds on a hypothesis-testing layer to EFA for confirming that links actually exist between the $k$ factors uncovered by EFA and the $p$ original variables


---

## PCA: the Algorithm

.center[
  ![:scale 30%](./pc1_proj.png)  ![:scale 30%](./pc1.png)
]

- The *score*, or the coordinate of the $i^{\rm th}$ observation along PC $j$ is
$$Z_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^p X_{ik} \phi_{kj}$$

  + $k$ represents the $k^{\rm th}$ variable or feature, i.e., the $k^{\rm th}$ column of your (predictor) data frame
  
  + $\phi$ is the rotation (or *loading*) matrix, which is normalized such that $\sum_{k=1}^p \phi_{kj}^2 = 1$

- *Note*: since we are "mixing axes" when doing PCA, it is almost always wise to standardize (or scale) the data frame before applying the algorithm


---

## PCA: Choosing the Number of Dimensions to Retain

- Ideally, we would choose some $M < p$ such that
$$x_{ij} = \sum_{m=1}^p z_{im}\phi_{jm} \approx \sum_{m=1}^M z_{im}\phi_{jm}$$

  + in other words, we hopefully wouldn't lose much ability to reconstruct the input data $X$ by dropping the last $p-M$ principal components, which we assume represent random variation in the data (i.e., just noise)

- One convention is to sum up the amount of variance explained in the first $M$ PCs, and adopt the smallest value of $M$ such that 90% or 95% or 99%, etc., of the overall variance is "explained" (i.e., via the right plot below, which shows cumulative proportion of variance explained)

- Another convention is to look for an "elbow" in the variance explained by each subsequent component (i.e., via the left plot below, a.k.a. the "scree plot")

.center[
  ![:scale 40%](./propvar.png)
]


---

## PCA: Example

```{r echo=FALSE}
file.path <- "https://github.com/FSKoerner/F25-36600-data/raw/refs/heads/main/Buzzard_DC1.Rdata"
load(url(file.path))
rm(file.path)
g  <- grepl("err", names(df))
df <- df[, !g]
df <- df[1:1000, c(1:6, 8)]
w  <- which(df[, 1] > 30)
df <- df[-w, ]
```

- Let's suppose we have a catalog of galaxies that contains measures of brightness in different wavelength bands, from `u` (for ultraviolet) to `z` and `y` (in the near-infrared)

```{r warning=FALSE,echo=FALSE,fig.height=5.5,fig.width=5.5,fig.align="center"}
suppressMessages(library(corrplot))
suppressMessages(library(tidyverse))
df %>% select(., -redshift) %>% cor(.) %>% corrplot(., method = "ellipse")
```

- The six brightness metrics are obviously highly correlated!


---

## PCA: Example

```{r}
pca.out <- prcomp(df[, -7], scale = TRUE) # do not include response variable!
v       <- pca.out$sdev^2
round(cumsum(v / sum(v)), 3)
```

- The first principal component explains 97.7% of the variance in the dataset: the data can safely be transformed from a six-dimensional space to a one-dimensional one with **minimal loss of statistical information**

- Let's print the loadings corresponding to each original variable for the PC that we retain:

```{r}
round(pca.out$rotation[, 1], 3)
```

- Here, we see that all the original variables contribute almost equally to the first PC (sign doesn't matter in this judgement)

  + we conclude that the predictor variables (for all intents and purposes) lie along a one-dimensional line in the native six-dimensional space, and that the orientation of the line is such that it spans all six of the original predictor variable axes


---

## PCA: Example

- What information is in the second PC?

```{r}
round(pca.out$rotation[, 1:2], 3)
```

- The second PC primarily maps to u-band magnitude; basically, the PC2 vector, orthogonal to the PC1 vector, points largely along the u-band axis, meaning there is *some* data variability along that axis which PC1 didn't "pick up"


---

## PC Regression

- Let's see how we would learn a principal components regression model using the distance of a galaxy from the Sun as our response variable:

<br>

```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=5.5,fig.width=5.5,fig.align="center"}
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = redshift)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "darkorchid", bins = 20)
```


---

## PC Regression

- Reminder: why are we doing this? 

  + to mitigate multicollinearity
  
  + and therefore, so we can "trust" the standard error estimates output by the linear model (say, via its `summary()`)


---

## PC Regression

- Let's split the data:

```{r}
set.seed(101)
s <- sample(nrow(df), round(0.7 * nrow(df)))
```

- The testing-set mean-squared error for a linear regression model learned in the data's native space is then:

```{r}
lm.out  <- lm(redshift ~ ., data = df, subset = s)
lm.pred <- predict(lm.out, newdata = df[-s, ])
mean((lm.pred - df$redshift[-s])^2)
```

- The testing-set mean-squared error for a PC regression model learned using all PCs:

```{r}
df.pc        <- data.frame(pca.out$x, df$redshift)
names(df.pc) <- c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "PC4", "PC5", "PC6", "y")
lm.out       <- lm(y ~ ., data = df.pc, subset = s)
lm.pred      <- predict(lm.out, newdata = df.pc[-s, ])
mean((lm.pred - df.pc$y[-s])^2)
```

- The testing-set MSEs are the same!


---

## PC Regression

- What happens if we learn a model with just the first two PCs, which should, by themselves, account for 99.8% of the data variability?

```{r}
lm.out  <- lm(y ~ PC1 + PC2, data = df.pc, subset = s)
lm.pred <- predict(lm.out, newdata = df.pc[-s, ])
mean((lm.pred - df.pc$y[-s])^2)
```

- The test-set MSE *increases*: there *can/will* be a trade-off between enhanced model interpretability and decreased model predictive ability if we summarily remove PCs
  
  + PC regression learns models with *rotated* predictor variable values; even with substantial sample sizes, this can markedly impact prediction results $-$ even if the retained PCs represent an overwhelming fraction of the cumulative variance


---

## PC Regression

- What happens if we use `bestglm`?

```{r warning=FALSE}
suppressMessages(library(bestglm))
bg.out <- bestglm(df.pc, IC = "BIC")
bg.out$BestModel
```

- **Takeaway**: the best set of PCs for visualization/intuition-building is not necessarily the best set of PCs for modeling!


---

## PC Regression

- Let's summarize the "best" model

```{r}
summary(bg.out$BestModel)$coefficients
```

- We see that if we change, e.g., PC2 by 1 unit, the distance will change by 0.024 $-$ but how does that change map back to the original variables? 

  + so it can be worthwhile to shift to PC coordinates to mitigate multicollinearity, **but** *crafting an inferential data story that refers back to the original variables can become very difficult* (and this is probably the most compelling reason that we wouldn't "just do" PC regression all the time!)
